blocks.prompt: The Bear That Sleeps Through Winter
blocks.text: A bear does not sleep the way you do. Your sleep lasts one night. A bear's winter sleep lasts for months. First the bear eats all fall. It puts on thick fat. Then it finds a den. A den can be a cave, or a hole under a big tree, or just a pile of leaves. The bear curls up small. Its heart slows down. It breathes slowly. Snow falls on top of the den. The bear stays warm inside. All winter it does not eat one bite. In spring, it walks out thin and hungry.

blocks.prompt: The Long Winter Sleep
blocks.text: Winter is hard on animals. The berries are gone. The fish are under ice. There is almost nothing to eat for months. Some animals fly south. Some grow thick coats and tough it out. The bear does something else. It quits. In the fall, a black bear eats like it will never eat again. It can pack away twenty thousand calories in one day, which is about ten times what you eat. All that food turns into fat. The fat is the bear's whole winter food supply. Then the bear digs a den. It curls up, and its body slows almost to a stop. Its heart can drop from fifty beats a minute to about ten. Sometimes it goes a full minute without taking a breath. For up to seven months it does not eat, does not drink, and does not go to the bathroom. In spring the bear walks out. It is thinner. It is hungry. But it is fine.

blocks.prompt: Seven Months Without a Meal
blocks.text: Every fall, a bear starts eating and does not stop. Biologists call this hyperphagia, which means over-eating. A black bear may spend twenty hours a day feeding and gain two pounds a day doing it. It is not being greedy. It is building the only food supply it will have until spring. When the snow comes, the bear digs a den and shuts down. Its heart rate falls from about fifty beats a minute to as few as eight. It may pause a whole minute between breaths. Its body burns fuel at about a quarter of its normal rate. But here is the strange part: its temperature only drops a few degrees. A ground squirrel hibernating nearby gets so cold it is nearly frozen. The bear stays warm enough to wake up and defend itself if something disturbs the den. Then there is the plumbing problem. You could not go seven months without a bathroom. The waste in your blood would poison you. The bear solves this by recycling. It takes the waste chemical urea, breaks it apart, and uses the pieces to build fresh protein. Nothing has to leave the body, because nothing is wasted. Strangest of all, mother bears give birth in the middle of this. Cubs arrive in January, blind and roughly the weight of a can of soda, and nurse in the dark while their mother dozes. When the den opens in spring, she walks out thin, and they walk out fat.

blocks.prompt: The Best Hibernator on Earth
blocks.text: For a long time, textbooks said bears do not really hibernate. The argument was about temperature. A hibernating ground squirrel is a startling thing to hold. Its body cools to just above freezing, its heart beats a few times a minute, and it is, for practical purposes, switched off. A denning bear does nothing so dramatic. Its temperature slips from about 100 degrees to the upper 80s, a drop you might get from a bad night's sleep. So the bear got demoted. Not a true hibernator, the books said. Just a deep sleeper. The books were wrong, and the reason is a matter of scale. A ground squirrel is small, and small bodies shed heat fast, so it has to go cold to save fuel. A bear is enormous and well insulated. It can cut its metabolism to a quarter of normal while staying warm, which is the whole point of hibernating. Measured by what actually matters, energy saved and time survived, the bear is arguably the best hibernator on the planet, and the warmth buys it something a squirrel cannot have. Disturb a denning bear and it wakes up. Disturb a hibernating squirrel and it needs hours to thaw. What a bear does inside the den is harder to explain than the sleeping. For up to seven months it does not eat, drink, urinate, or defecate. Your body could not manage a week of that. Urea, the waste your kidneys flush out in urine, would build up in your blood and kill you. The bear does not flush it. Bacteria in its gut split the urea apart, and the bear reuses the nitrogen to build new protein. It is drinking its own waste, chemically speaking, and coming out healthier for it. It also does not fall apart. Put a person in bed for seven months and they lose muscle and bone. The bear emerges in spring with its skeleton intact and most of its muscle still on it. It has lost fat, and almost nothing else. None of this is fully understood. That is exactly why kidney specialists, bone researchers, and diabetes labs all keep files on bears.

6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Bear That Sleeps Through Winter

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Hyperphagia can run 20 hours a day
Insulin sensitivity flips on a seasonal schedule
PTEN: a protein linked to the bear's insulin switch
Metabolic rate falls to roughly 25% of normal
Gut bacteria hydrolyze urea; nitrogen gets reused
Emerges with skeleton and muscle largely intact

blocks.prompt: What the Bear Does in the Dark
blocks.text: Twice a year a bear performs a metabolic maneuver that no human doctor can reproduce, and it does it without a hospital, a monitor, or a single conscious decision. Start in autumn. The bear enters hyperphagia, a state of driven overeating that can run twenty hours a day. A grizzly fattening on salmon or whitebark pine seeds may take in tens of thousands of calories daily and gain several pounds in twenty-four hours. In a human, this would be catastrophic. Weight like that, laid on that fast, would push blood sugar out of control and drive the body toward diabetes. The bear gains it and stays healthy. In autumn its cells remain exquisitely sensitive to insulin, packing fuel into fat as fast as it arrives. Then, as the bear dens, a switch flips and the same cells turn insulin resistant, which stops them from burning the fat too quickly. In spring the switch flips back. Researchers have narrowed part of this to a single protein, PTEN, that the bear's fat cells appear to turn down and up on schedule. Human bodies possess the same machinery. Ours simply does not do that. Now the den. For as long as seven months the bear does not eat, drink, urinate, or defecate. Its metabolic rate falls to roughly a quarter of normal, its heart can slow to eight beats a minute, and it may go a full minute between breaths. Yet its core temperature drops only from about 100 degrees Fahrenheit to the upper 80s. That modest cooling is why textbooks once refused the bear the title of true hibernator, reserving it for small mammals like the arctic ground squirrel, which chills to below freezing. The objection has not aged well. Hibernation is a strategy for surviving scarcity on stored fuel, and by that measure the bear is the most accomplished hibernator known. It also gains something the squirrel forfeits: a warm bear can wake, stand, and fight within seconds. A frozen squirrel needs hours. Then there is the waste. Urea is the nitrogen-bearing byproduct of breaking down protein, and your kidneys spend your whole life clearing it. Let it accumulate and it will kill you. The denning bear never clears it. Instead, bacteria in its gut hydrolyze the urea, and the bear captures the freed nitrogen and reassembles it into new protein. The waste stream is closed. Nothing goes out because nothing is discarded, and this is a large part of why the bear does not waste away: it is quietly rebuilding itself from its own garbage all winter. That rebuilding shows up in the numbers. Immobilize a human for seven months and the losses are severe, on the order of a percent of bone mass per month, plus substantial muscle. The bear lies still for a comparable stretch and emerges with its skeleton essentially unchanged and most of its muscle intact. It has burned fat, and mostly only fat. Somewhere in the middle of all this, a pregnant female gives birth, in the dark, to cubs weighing less than a pound, and nurses them for months on a body that is taking in nothing at all. Every one of these tricks describes a disease we cannot fix. Osteoporosis is bone lost without load. Muscle atrophy is disuse. Chronic kidney disease is urea unremoved. Type 2 diabetes is insulin resistance arriving at the wrong time. The bear does all four on purpose, on a calendar, and reverses them by April. The instructions are written in a genome that is largely shared with ours. Reading them is another matter.
